newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Republicans optimistic on budget, tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Republicans optimistic on budget, tax cuts.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and congressional Republicans said on Monday they were optimistic that a budget and tax deal could be struck soon, but negotiators were still working on one of the toughest issues, a new children's health insurance programme.
"This is an historic opportunity. It can be the achievement of a generation," the president told a bipartisan meeting of the nation's governors. "I believe we're on the verge of achieving it."
Clinton outlined before the National Governors' Association in Las Vegas what he felt must be in the final package, all of them thorny issues as yet unsettled.

"It's clear to me that it must have a child tax credit available for working families that need it," he said. "It should include $24 billion for children's health care. It should ... include a tobacco tax to help pay for that health care, and it should preserve the fiscal integrity of the budget," he said.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott turned up the pressure on the president to sign off on the final budget and tax bills this week to enable votes in Congress before they leave on Friday for a month-long vacation. Agreement today would allow votes to start Wednesday and final passage by the weekend.

"If we don't do it now our relationship between the administration and Congress will deteriorate rapidly. It will be much, much more difficult to get it done in September," the Mississippi Republican warned.

He mentioned the other pressing legislation that Congress needs to address this fall including Clinton's nominations, annual spending bills, and other legislation. "Everything just gets completely gummed up," he said.

Republican leaders Lott and House Speaker Newt Gingrich sent a very different message to the governors, appealing for their help in convincing Clinton to back down on applying fair labour standards to people hired off the welfare rolls and to ease up on proposed coverage of children in a new health plan.

Republicans, and many governors, want states to have broad latitude to design their own health programmes as part of a new federal plan to cover uninsured children. The administration has been pushing for a uniform, nationwide benfits package.
Sources said the child care could cost $24 billion, up from $16 billion as originally proposed and would partially be paid for with a tobacco tax increase.

Lawmakers and congressional sources said Republicans have generally accepted that tobacco taxes will be increased, probably by 15 cents per pack. The Senate had orignally approved a 20 cent hike but this could not get past House objections.
While both sides stressed that no agreement would be final until all of the details were worked out, many of the broad parameters were in place.

Once enacted, the plan would give taxpayers the first tax cut in 16 years, a $85 billion tax break that would include a $500 per child tax credit, expand retirement accounts, help pay for higher education and allow investors to pay lower taxes on capital gains.
